description: TerraNex is a multidisciplinary team interested in using Earth observation, agriculture, data science, artificial intelligence, and software to solve real-world environmental challenges.
summary: Dawra AI ("dawra" means "rotation" in Arabic) is a working bilingual (English and Egyptian Arabic) web app that helps small farmers in dry, salty areas choose a 3-year crop rotation. It compares the farmer's current rotation with plans found by an optimisation algorithm (NSGA-II), stress-tests each plan against bad climate years and 2050s futures, and explains each plan in simple language. The farmer and extension officer decide. It addresses the Field Shift challenge. In Ras Sudr, South Sinai, crops need about 1,912 mm of water a year but only about 47 mm of rain falls, so farms depend on salty wells, and the highly saline aquifer area rose from 52% (1996) to 83% (2022). Dawra AI uses NASA POWER (crop water needs), Landsat and Sentinel-2 (real land use) and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 (2050s tests). For our one real pilot farm (F001), the recommended plan gives an estimated +26% net profit over 3 years and 11% less well water (13,588 vs 15,260 m³). The profit is an estimate because 19 of 21 price rows are estimates. This is a prototype: one pilot farm, no field test with farmers yet. Next step: a pilot with farmers and the Desert Research Center in Ras Sudr.
details:
What it does?

Dawra AI is a live web app that simulates a farmer's current rotation, searches for better 3-year plans, stress-tests each plan against bad and future climates, and explains each plan in plain language (English and Egyptian Arabic). It suggests and explains; the farmer and extension officer decide.

  • Main use (input → process → output)
    Input: farm profile (area, well salinity, water per day, irrigation type, livestock, last crop, crops to avoid) and the farmer's priorities (profit, water saving, salt tolerance, soil health, market, climate risk). In the app the user can change well salinity (5–12 dS/m), daily water (40/60/90 m³) and the priority profile.
    Process: NSGA-II searches crop choice and irrigated area for all 6 seasons (19 crops, the well's daily water as a hard limit) for three goals: profit (EGP), water (m³) and soil health. It picks four plans: highest profit, water saver, soil builder, and the best balance for this farmer (TOPSIS). Each plan is replayed in 5,400 futures: 45 years of NASA climate, +1/+2 °C, −10/−20% rain, NASA CMIP6 2050s, and a saltier well, each with 100%, 70% or 40% of the needed leaching water.
    Output: side-by-side plan cards (profit, water, soil score, robustness), P10–P90 profit range, a card back with the explanation (why, NASA evidence, benefits, information gaps, risks), a What-if lab with sliders, and a simple Farmer mode (3 questions → 1 plan in plain Arabic).
    How the data supports it. NASA POWER gives the FAO-56 reference water need (about 1,912 mm/yr) and effective rain (about 47 mm/yr), and its 45-year record is resampled to build the climate futures. Landsat shows green farmland growing from 13 ha (1990) to 1,302 ha (2025) over the same salty aquifer. NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 creates two 2050s futures. Sentinel-2 gives 122 cultivated fields (125 ha) and their season patterns.
  • Pilot results: (farm F001: 5 feddan ≈ 2.1 ha, well 8.35 dS/m, 60 m³/day, drip)
  • Current rotation: 125,325 EGP, 15,260 m³, soil score 52, robustness 32%.
  • Best balance (recommended): 158,385 EGP (estimated +26%), 13,588 m³ (−11%), soil 55, robustness 49%. It earns 11.7 EGP per m³ of water vs 8.2.
  • Highest profit: 360,515 EGP (+188%) but 34,863 m³ (+128%), more than a 60 m³/day well can supply every year, so it is shown but not recommended.
  • Water saver: 109,808 EGP (−12%), 8,572 m³ (−44%), robustness 8%.
  • Soil builder: 131,448 EGP (+5%), 28,168 m³ (+85%), soil score 71.
  • Key finding: the current rotation is the most fragile. With only 70% of the leaching water, salt builds up in almost every future. Climate variation moves profit only about ±3%, so leaching practice is the biggest risk.
  • Benefits and goals: More income per drop of well water; protect soil and aquifer by tracking soil salt season by season; plan for climate change before committing; transparency (every number traces to NASA data, a cited local source S1–S18, or one of 139 documented assumptions); reach (phone-friendly, bilingual, Farmer mode).
  • Tools, languages, software: Python 3.11 (pandas, numpy, pymoo, scikit-learn, shapely, Google Earth Engine Python API, pytest with 66 tests). Methods: FAO-56 Penman–Monteith, FAO-29 leaching and salt tolerance, Maas–Hoffman salinity–yield model, block-bootstrap climate resampling, TOPSIS. Web app: Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, framer-motion, three.js, Recharts, Leaflet, hosted on Vercel, reading pre-computed JSON files (4.8 MB), so no server-side Python. Playwright tests; Lighthouse (home 99 desktop / 90 mobile, accessibility 100). No special hardware.
  • Evidence and validation: 15 pass, 9 fail (kept and explained), 4 calibrated, 1 not testable. NASA POWER from the API matches the team's file exactly; our FAO-56 code reproduces the textbook example (3.9 mm/day). Wheat tested on an independent local result: error −15%, inside our ±20% target. Kept failures include NASA POWER night temperatures about 1.8 °C warmer than the station, and our FAO-29 water need being 73% above one local trial. Of 106 assumptions changed by ±20%, 11 change at least one plan choice.
  • Working now (prototype): Full pipeline from NASA data to plan cards; live bilingual app with 5 tabs and Farmer mode; 15 pre-computed farm settings (5 well salinities × 3 water supplies) with 5 priority profiles each; What-if sliders and the 5,400-future stress test; Landsat and Sentinel-2 evidence on the map.
  • Limitations: This is one pilot farm (F001) and there has been no field test with farmers yet; the next step is a pilot with farmers and the Desert Research Center station in Ras Sudr. Soil data comes from one research station; 19 of 21 crop price/cost rows include an estimate (flagged in the app); leaching achieved, fallow salt rise, residue carbon and legume nitrogen are literature assumptions; MODIS MOD16 ET has no data over this desert. All results are model results, not field-tested outcomes.
  • Future plans (not built yet): Pilot with farmers and the Desert Research Center station in Ras Sudr; real market prices updated each season; field-level plans from each farm's own satellite history and soil test; SMS/WhatsApp Farmer mode; extension to North Sinai, Red Sea and North Coast.
  • AI/SI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code, tests and documentation from the team's instructions; Kokoro-82M generated the English voice-over; Canva AI styled the team graphic. The idea, pilot site, local data and decisions are the team's own. Prompts and instructions are kept in the repo (CLAUDE.md, PROMPTS.md).
